John Day
jon dā
n. (John Day, 1522–1584, London printer of Foxe's Acts and Monuments)
Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Day, from Old English daeg, a byname.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

John Day was the best-equipped printer in Elizabethan England and the publisher of the book that shaped English Protestant self-understanding for three centuries. He printed Foxe's Acts and Monuments in 1563 and in four further editions, each enormous, each heavily illustrated with woodcuts of the burnings, each a commercial undertaking of a size no other English printer could have attempted. He also printed Tyndale's and Frith's works, the first English church music books, and the first book printed in Anglo-Saxon types, which he had cut so that Archbishop Parker could publish the Old English homilies and show that the medieval English church had not always taught what Rome now taught. Day was imprisoned under Mary and had to print secretly under a false imprint. His woodcuts are the reason the Marian burnings are visible to the English imagination at all. “Therefore whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light” (Luk 12:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines woodcut as an engraving on wood, and imprint as the name of the printer with the place and date of publication.

expand to see more

WOOD'CUT, n. An engraving on wood, or a print from such an engraving.

IM'PRINT, n. The name of the printer, with the place and date of publication, printed in a book.

EN'GRAVING, n. The act or art of cutting figures or letters on hard substances; a print from an engraved block.

SAX'ON, a. Pertaining to the Saxons or to their language.

Modern Corruption

The press behind Foxe's book, and the woodcuts that fixed the Marian fires in English memory.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the dismissal of Foxe as propaganda, which is an easy charge and a lazy one. The book has faults: it is partisan, it is credulous in places, and Foxe sometimes prints what he was told. It also quotes documents at enormous length, including the registers of the bishops who conducted the trials, and modern scholarship checking those citations has generally found them sound. A book may be an advocate's and still be a record.

The principle to recover is that God has arranged for things done in private to become public, and that the church's keeping of such records is a participation in that arrangement rather than a vindictiveness. “For there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed; neither hid, that shall not be known” (Luk 12:2). The exposure is described as the work of light: “all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light” (Eph 5:13). And the slain are already counted under the altar (Rev 6:9); a printer only makes the count legible.

Greek apokalupto (G601), to uncover, to reveal; phaneroo (G5319), to make manifest.

Greek kerusso (G2784) — to proclaim, to herald publicly; Luke 12:3.

Greek phaneroo (G5319) — to make manifest, to make visible; Ephesians 5:13.

Greek marturia (G3141) — testimony, witness, evidence; Revelation 6:9.

Usage

"“whatsoever ye have spoken in darkness shall be heard in the light” (Luk 12:3) — London, 1563 and after."

"“there is nothing covered, that shall not be revealed” (Luk 12:2) — the woodcuts of the burnings."

"“the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) — five editions, each enormous."
